questions.q: By default, which rows does df.duplicated() mark as True?
options: Every row that has a copy, including the first one
The second and later copies of a row that matches an earlier row on all columns
Only rows whose first column repeats
questions.explain: keep="first" is the default, so the first occurrence is treated as the original and later exact matches are flagged.

questions.q: Two rows share order_id 5004 but have amounts of 200 and 210. What are they?
options: An exact duplicate that drop_duplicates() should remove
A conflict: same key with different values that should be investigated before dropping anything
questions.explain: Same key with different values is a conflicting record. Silently keeping one means guessing which value is right.

questions.q: Which call shows every row involved in a key-based duplicate, including the first occurrence?
questions.explain: keep=False marks all members of each duplicated group, so filtering with it displays the full set of conflicting rows.

questions.q: A state column contains 'GA', 'ga', 'GA ' and 'Georgia'. Which cleaning sequence produces one consistent value?
questions.explain: Strip removes the trailing space, upper unifies case, and the dictionary maps the spelled-out variant to the code. title() alone would leave 'Ga' and 'Georgia' as different values.

questions.q: Why should you standardize text before calling drop_duplicates()?
options: drop_duplicates() only works on uppercase text
Standardizing makes the DataFrame smaller in memory
Rows that differ only in spacing or capitalization will not be detected as duplicates until their spelling matches
questions.explain: Duplicate detection compares exact values. 'Ana Ruiz' and '  ana ruiz' are different strings until you clean them.
